content: The comparison of outcomes between children breastfed for more than one year and those breastfed for less than one year was a key focus of the studies. However, many studies were excluded for various reasons. The second most common reason for exclusion was the use of a case-control design (90 studies), which was not representative of the population. Twelve studies lacked a comparison (control) group, and seven studies did not provide data on outcomes relevant to this review. In seven studies, other co-interventions were present alongside breastfeeding, making it impossible to isolate the effect of breastfeeding duration alone. Four studies involved participants who were not healthy, as they either had a disease condition or were at risk of developing a disease prior to breastfeeding exposure. In four studies, the breastfeeding durations in the exposure and/or control groups did not meet the defined criteria, and in two studies, breastfeeding exposure coexisted with bottle or formula feeding. One article was a literature review on prolonged breastfeeding beyond one year, and another study did not provide detailed data relevant to the review's objectives. The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed using the Risk of Bias for Nutrition Observational Studies (RoB-NObs) tool. The severity of bias was categorized as low, moderate, severe, critical, or unclear. All 146 included studies had some risk of bias due to confounding, with 112 studies classified as having serious risk. Two studies (Danial 2017 and Rajaei 2016) did not provide information on confounding and were classified as having unclear risk of bias. Regarding participant selection, 4% of studies were at low risk of bias, while 98 studies were at moderate risk. Four studies (Derakhshan 2017, Fredriksson 2007, Helderman 2006, Tryggvadottir 2001) were classified as having severe risk of bias due to issues with participant selection and timing of exposure and follow-up. One study (Fonseca 2010) was classified as having unclear risk of bias due to insufficient information. In terms of exposure classification, 48% of studies were at low risk of bias, while 79 were at moderate risk. Four studies (Butt 2014, Danial 2017, Fonseca 2010, Hansstein 2016) were assessed as having serious risk of bias due to unreliable methods for defining exposure or potential misclassification. For bias due to departure from intended exposure, 22 studies were at low risk, 91 at moderate risk, and 29 at serious risk. Four studies (Danial 2017, Intusoma 2016, Rajaei 2016, Sichieri 2003) had unclear risk due to insufficient information. Regarding missing exposure or outcome data, 75 studies were classified as having low or moderate risk, while eight studies (Ardic 2018, Butt 2014, Chetwynd 2017, Girard 2019, Helderman 2006, Li 2020, Oddy 2010, Tanaka 2012) were at serious risk due to inappropriate handling of missing data. About 10% of studies had unclear risk due to insufficient information. For outcome measurement, nearly all studies (98%) were at low risk of bias. One study each was classified as having moderate risk (Fonseca 2010), serious risk (Hansstein 2016), and critical risk (Chetwynd 2017) due to issues with outcome assessment methods. Regarding selection of reported results, 89% of studies were at low risk, 12 at moderate risk, and four (Chetwynd 2017, Fagerhaug 2013, Liese 2001, Lee 2016) at serious risk due to selective reporting based on results. The effects of prolonged breastfeeding into the second year on child development, intelligence, cognition, and behavior were assessed. The age of children at the time of developmental assessment ranged from 32 months to 18 years, with one study (Lima 2019) evaluating intelligence in adults at 30 years of age. There was significant clinical heterogeneity in terms of age at assessment, outcome definitions, and measurement scales. Two prospective cohort studies (Kim 2020a and Oddy 2010) from high-income countries (Korea and Australia) provided quantitative data on developmental delay in children breastfed into the second year compared to those who discontinued breastfeeding before one year. Kim 2020a assessed development at multiple time points, but the certainty of evidence was graded as very low, indicating uncertainty about whether prolonged breastfeeding prevents developmental delay. Three studies provided subgroup data for breastfeeding duration in the continued breastfeeding group (12–18 months and 18–24 months). However, the certainty of evidence remained very low. Lee 2016 assessed the effect of breastfeeding duration on the Korean version of the Bayley Scale of Infant Development, but no significant differences were observed between children breastfed for 9–11 months and those breastfed for more than 12 months. Jiang 2011 evaluated the effect of breastfeeding duration on various cognitive test scores but did not provide standard deviations, making the results unsuitable for quantitative analysis. Belfort 2013 studied the effect of breastfeeding duration on intelligence scores at 3 and 7 years of age, using regression analyses to assess the impact on IQ points per month of breastfeeding. However, the certainty of evidence was very low, suggesting uncertainty about the cognitive benefits of prolonged breastfeeding. Nutritional anthropometry outcomes, such as underweight, stunting, and wasting, were also assessed. Seven studies provided data on underweight odds in children exposed to continued breastfeeding. The certainty of evidence was very low, indicating uncertainty about whether prolonged breastfeeding increases the risk of underweight in children under five. Three studies provided data on stunting, but the certainty of evidence was also very low. Two studies reported on wasting, with very low certainty of evidence for increased odds of wasting among children breastfed during the second year. Z-scores for weight-for-age, height-for-age, and weight-for-height were evaluated in some studies, but no significant associations were found between breastfeeding duration and these nutritional indices. Regarding overweight and obesity, 28 studies provided data on these outcomes in children and adolescents aged 2–18 years. The certainty of evidence was very low, with no consistent pattern observed between breastfeeding duration and the risk of overweight or obesity. Some studies suggested a lower probability of obesity with longer breastfeeding duration, but the evidence was not robust.
